title: Linear algebra at exponential scale via tensor network dimension reduction
authors: Chris Camaño, Ethan N. Epperly, Raphael A. Meyer, Joel A. Tropp
abstract: Many problems in modern scientific computing are challenging because of a \emph{curse of dimension}, where their mathematical formulation involves objects whose dimension is \emph{exponential} in the nominal "size" of the problem. Tensor networks can provide a compact representation for exponentially large vectors and matrices that arise in applications, but these representations do not always lead to reliable algorithms. This paper develops and analyzes techniques for randomized dimension reduction of tensor network data. These techniques support a suite of efficient algorithms for provably solving exponential-scale linear algebra problems, including trace estimation and eigenvalue approximation. The paper includes several stylized illustrations from quantum many-body physics with ambient dimension up to $2^{200}$.
summary: This paper introduces randomized dimension reduction techniques using random Matrix Product States (rMPS) to solve linear algebra problems on exponentially large matrices arising in quantum physics. By projecting these high-dimensional operators onto a low-rank rMPS subspace, it enables efficient computation of observables like partition functions and traces that were previously computationally inaccessible.
main_problem: The core challenge is solving linear algebra problems whose computational resources scale exponentially with system size due to the curse of dimension.
main_result: Randomized dimension reduction techniques, specifically using random Matrix Product States (rMPS), allow for provably efficient estimation of quantities like partition functions and traces at exponential scales.
method: The authors develop and analyze randomized algorithms that replace direct computation with low-dimensional projections derived from rMPS test matrices. These methods adapt standard linear algebra estimators (like the Girard–Hutchinson estimator) to the tensor network structure.
model_or_system: The primary physical model is quantum many-body physics, exemplified by calculating the partition function $Z( eta)$ for Hamiltonians like the PTFIM, which leads to exponentially large matrices ($2^n 	imes 2^n$). The mathematical framework relies on representing these operators and states using Matrix Product States (MPS) and Operators (MPO).
key_observables: Partition function $Z( eta)$, trace estimation $	ext{Tr}(e^{- eta H})$, eigenvalue approximations, and various norms ($\|A\|_*$, $\|A\|_F$).
important_parameters: System size exponent ($n$), local dimension ($d$), bond dimension ($\chi$), and the ratio $\chi/n$ which dictates algorithmic scaling.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that rMPS test matrices provide a sufficiently good embedding (subspace injection) to preserve necessary geometric properties for accurate estimation, particularly when the bond dimension $\chi \gtrsim n$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 demonstrates rMPS-based trace estimation for $n=70$ requiring only megabytes of storage. Figure 2 shows convergence of variance estimators towards Gaussian behavior as $\chi/n$ increases. Figure 3 compares the accuracy of the rMPS Girard–Hutchinson estimator against theoretical bounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the exponential scaling problem, then introducing tensor networks (MPS/MPO) for representation, developing randomized dimension reduction via rMPSs, and finally applying these tools to specific linear algebra tasks like trace estimation and Nyström approximation with rigorous error bounds.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides concrete, scalable numerical machinery to tackle quantum many-body problems that are intractable for exact diagonalization or standard tensor methods due to the sheer size of the Hilbert space.

Figure 1 shows the results. For tensor order n = 70, the rMPS-based implementation of XNysTrace can estimate the partition function to 1% relative error using megabytes of storage and minutes of computation. By using rMPSs and efficient tensor network methods to store and apply the Hamiltonian H, we can extend the XNysTrace algorithm to perform trace estimation at exponential scale. As a baseline, we compare against the performance of Gaussian–Kronecker vectors that have the form ω = ϕ(1) ⊗· · · ⊗ϕ(n) with iid Gaussian ϕ(i) ∼NR(0, I2). Gaussian–Kronecker vectors are widely used in the literature [2,4,15,17,18,74,75,101], and they also enable us to implement XNysTrace at exponential scale....
